title: Living Languages. Lasting Connections.
deck: Eleven languages. Eleven distinct histories of cultural endurance, unequal power, and renewal. An exploration of what happens when a language loses its place in everyday life—and what it takes to make room for its future.

sections.heading: A Language Is Never Just a Collection of Words
sections.body:
Imagine a child beginning school and discovering that the language spoken around the family table is unwelcome in the classroom.

The words that child learned from parents and grandparents—the words used for comfort, affection, questions, and stories—suddenly carry a different meaning. In the world outside the home, they can become a source of embarrassment, disadvantage, or even punishment.

For some communities, this was not an imagined situation. It was part of their history.

Across different places and periods, languages have been driven from classrooms, excluded from public institutions, discouraged in workplaces, or treated as barriers to opportunity. Children have been punished for speaking their mother tongues. Families have been pressured to raise the next generation in a more politically or economically powerful language. Entire communities have watched the places where their languages could be used grow steadily smaller.

Yet many of these languages remain alive.

Not because their survival was inevitable, but because people continued to speak, teach, write, remember, organize, and create through them.

**This series is about those histories—and the people determined that their languages should have a future.**

sections.heading: What We Lose When a Language Falls Silent
sections.body:
Every language represents generations of human experience.

It carries ordinary conversations and extraordinary literature. It gives names to landscapes, plants, animals, relationships, and practices. It preserves stories about where people came from, how they understand their surroundings, and what previous generations considered important enough to pass on.

Some languages contain highly specialized knowledge of local environments, agricultural practices, navigation, family relationships, or cultural traditions. Others preserve long literary histories that reveal how communities have understood politics, spirituality, humor, grief, and belonging across centuries.

But the value of a language is not determined by how ancient it is, how many people speak it, or whether it possesses a famous literary tradition.

A language also matters because people use it to live.

To greet a neighbor. To comfort a child. To tell a joke that works only in the original words. To disagree, celebrate, work, teach, and describe an ordinary afternoon.

Translation can communicate a great deal. It can also fail to preserve the full cultural associations, historical references, and subtle meanings of an expression.

When a language stops passing naturally between generations, some of those connections become harder to sustain. Knowledge may survive in recordings, books, or translations, but access to it can change profoundly when fewer people can understand and use the language themselves.

Language loss is therefore more than a change in vocabulary.

It can alter the relationship between generations, communities, cultural knowledge, and the places people call home.

sections.heading: How Does a Language Become Endangered?
sections.body:
Languages do not all become threatened for the same reasons.

Political conquest and colonization have sometimes imposed dominant languages through government, education, and law. In other circumstances, migration, economic changes, discrimination, urbanization, and the unequal prestige of different languages have reshaped how families and communities communicate.

Schools have often played a particularly powerful role.

A school can help a language flourish by teaching children to read, write, think, and learn through it. But it can also accelerate language shift when children are taught that their home language has no legitimate place in education.

In some historical settings, children were punished for speaking the language they knew best. In others, punishment was not required: qualifications, employment, and social advancement were so strongly associated with a dominant language that families felt compelled to change what they spoke at home.

These decisions cannot always be understood as free preferences.

When parents believe their children must abandon a language to obtain an education, avoid discrimination, or find work, the resulting language shift reflects the pressures of the society around them.

Nor does every threatened language move steadily toward disappearance. Some have maintained substantial speaker populations despite institutional pressure. Others have experienced severe disruption in the transmission of their language to children. Some are now producing new generations of speakers through community-led education.

There is no single pattern of decline, and no single formula for recovery.

What these histories reveal is that **a language's future depends not only on whether people value it, but on whether society gives them meaningful opportunities to use it.**

sections.heading: Eleven Languages. Eleven Different Experiences.
sections.body:
The WPMTest Living Languages Series follows eleven languages and language varieties across the Pacific, Europe, East Asia, and the Middle East.

Their circumstances differ significantly.

**ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi — Hawaiian**  
The language of an independent kingdom whose place in education was severely disrupted after the overthrow of its government. Its modern renewal is closely connected to the determination of families, kūpuna, teachers, and Hawaiian-language immersion movements.

**Cymraeg — Welsh**  
A language with centuries of literary and community life that endured institutional stigma, including documented punishment of Welsh-speaking schoolchildren, and became the focus of sustained campaigns for education and public-language rights.

**Gaelg — Manx**  
The language of the Isle of Man, whose decline in traditional native-speaker transmission did not end the efforts of people determined to teach and speak it. Its modern story challenges the assumption that a language must remain lost once a generation of traditional speakers passes away.

**Gàidhlig — Scottish Gaelic**  
A language shaped by the histories of the Highlands and Islands, displacement, migration, educational exclusion, and community resilience. Its future depends on more than recognition: it depends on opportunities to live through Gaelic.

**Gaeilge — Irish**  
A language with an extraordinary literary history whose speakers experienced centuries of political, social, and economic pressure. Modern efforts connect education, public rights, cultural expression, and the continuing life of Irish-speaking communities.

**Català — Catalan**  
A language spoken by millions across several European territories, including Andorra, Catalonia, and other communities. Its history illustrates how cultural and literary vitality can coexist with political restrictions and continuing debates over language rights.

**Tâi-gí — Taiwanese Taigi**  
A major language of everyday communication and cultural life in Taiwan that experienced pressure from Mandarin-dominant language policies and remains central to efforts to strengthen intergenerational transmission and public use.

**四縣客語 — Sixian Hakka**  
An important Hakka variety in Taiwan, with distinct linguistic features and educational resources. Its future is connected to opportunities for Hakka-speaking families and communities to sustain their languages across generations.

**海陸客語 — Hailu Hakka**  
Another important Hakka variety in Taiwan, with its own pronunciation patterns and community history. Its inclusion recognizes that related language varieties are not interchangeable and deserve attention in their own right.

**溫州話 — Wenzhounese**  
A distinctive variety of Wu Chinese associated with Wenzhou and its diaspora. Its story invites readers to examine what linguistic diversity means in a society where a national standard language has considerable institutional influence.

**کوردیی ناوەندی — Sorani Kurdish**  
A major Kurdish language variety used across parts of Iraq and Iran and in diaspora communities. Its literary and cultural history reflects the complexity of maintaining linguistic identity across political borders and differing language policies.

These are not eleven versions of the same story.

Some have millions of speakers. Others are rebuilding pathways for learning after severe disruption. Some are languages in their own right within established linguistic classifications; others are named varieties whose specific identities and writing conventions deserve to be respected.

Their inclusion does not imply that all eleven are equally endangered, that all experienced identical forms of suppression, or that every community has the same goals.

**The common thread is not disappearance. It is the relationship between language, power, cultural continuity, and the right to use one's own words.**

sections.heading: The People Who Keep Languages Alive
sections.body:
Language revitalization can sound like an abstract institutional project.

In practice, it often begins with ordinary people taking on extraordinary responsibilities.

A parent decides to raise a child in a language they themselves had few opportunities to use. An elder shares stories and expressions with younger speakers. A teacher develops lessons despite a shortage of materials. A writer produces books that future generations will be able to read. A community organizes classes, creates recordings, or establishes an immersion school.

Sometimes the work means rebuilding something that was deliberately weakened.

Sometimes it means protecting something that has never stopped being spoken but is becoming harder to use in everyday settings.

And sometimes it means restoring the confidence to speak a language that previous generations were taught to hide.

Language revitalization is not simply about preserving recordings or filling dictionaries. Those resources can be invaluable, but living languages need living relationships.

They need children who can answer their grandparents. They need people who can learn, work, form friendships, raise families, and participate in community life through the language.

They need places where speaking the language is ordinary rather than exceptional.

That work belongs first and foremost to the communities themselves.

Their priorities, knowledge, and leadership should shape how their languages are taught, represented, and supported.

sections.heading: Why Recognition Is Not Enough
sections.body:
Legal recognition can represent an enormous achievement.

A language that was once discouraged in schools may become a language of instruction. A language previously excluded from government offices may gain formal rights in public services. Broadcasting, publishing, and digital resources can expand its visibility.

But a language can be visible without being secure.

A bilingual sign does not guarantee a conversation. A school qualification does not guarantee that graduates will use the language with their friends. A law cannot, on its own, recreate the community relationships disrupted over generations.

For a language to thrive, people need both the ability and the opportunity to use it.

That means looking beyond formal recognition to the conditions of everyday life: housing and migration, community continuity, employment, education, family transmission, social confidence, and the resources available to speakers.

The difference matters.

Language policy can open doors. Communities need the means to walk through them.

sections.heading: Why a Typing Website Is Telling These Stories
sections.body:
WPMTest began with a straightforward purpose: helping people develop typing speed and accuracy.

But a keyboard is also a place where language enters the digital world.

Every day, people use keyboards to send messages, write stories, complete schoolwork, communicate with colleagues, record knowledge, and stay connected to the people who matter to them.

For widely supported languages, much of this infrastructure is easy to take for granted.

For others, accurate written use may require particular keyboard layouts, diacritics, scripts, fonts, software support, or educational materials.

Digital inclusion is not a substitute for community language transmission. But practical access to a language's writing system matters when people want to use that language in contemporary life.

That is where WPMTest can make a modest contribution.

The Living Languages Series combines carefully sourced historical introductions with opportunities to encounter and practise written language.

It invites visitors to understand why a language has faced pressure, how communities have responded, what challenges remain, and where to find additional resources.

The purpose is not to claim that typing a few characters preserves a language.

It does not.

A keyboard exercise cannot restore generations of interrupted transmission, replace fluent speakers, or confer cultural knowledge and belonging.

But it can create a moment of attention.

It can encourage a visitor to notice an unfamiliar writing convention, learn the history behind a language, and seek out the communities and resources that sustain it.

**We cannot measure the value of a language in words per minute. We can choose to give its written form the care it deserves.**

sections.heading: Explore the History. Then Look Beyond the Page.
sections.body:
Each article in the Living Languages Series introduces the language, the historical forces that shaped its position, and the people and institutions working to strengthen its future.

Readers will find historical accounts, selected timelines, information about contemporary language efforts, guidance on written forms, and references for further investigation.

Where appropriate, a related typing activity offers a way to practise characters, names, or verified passages.

The Hawaiian pathway currently includes dedicated practice passages. The other ten begin with introductory character and name-copying activities, together with the option to supply independently verified text.

These activities should not be mistaken for complete language courses or speaker-reviewed sentence collections.

Anyone interested in learning a language more deeply should seek authentic listening material, suitable instruction, and opportunities to learn from speakers and community-led organizations.

The stories are an invitation to begin—not a claim that the work can be completed here.

sections.heading: The Future of a Language Is Written by Its People
sections.body:
There is a temptation to tell language histories as tragedies with predictable endings.

A language is suppressed. Its speakers decline. The last generation disappears. A record remains.

But that is not the only story.

In Hawaiʻi, families helped build new educational pathways through their ancestral language. In Wales, generations challenged the exclusion of Welsh from public life. In Scotland, educators and communities continue working to make Gaelic a language children can learn and use.

Elsewhere, teachers, writers, parents, activists, and young speakers are creating their own responses to very different circumstances.

Their work does not erase what happened before.

It does something more important.

It refuses to let past injustice determine every possibility of the future.

A living language is not merely an artifact inherited from history. It is something people continue to shape through conversation, education, creativity, care, and everyday use.

The languages in this series belong to the people who speak and sustain them. Their futures cannot be guaranteed by legislation, technology, or good intentions alone.

But they can be supported.

And the first step toward meaningful support is understanding why they matter.

**Eleven languages. Eleven living stories. Countless reasons to keep listening.**

*Start with the history. Stay for the language. Make space for every voice.*

---

### Continue Exploring

Discover all eleven language pathways, from Hawaiian and Welsh to Scottish Gaelic, Taiwanese Taigi, Wenzhounese, and Sorani Kurdish.

Each story offers historical context, selected sources, and an introduction to careful written practice.

**Additional Learning Resources**

Typing is only one part of learning a language. Listening, conversation, reading, education, and community participation are essential to meaningful progress.

Glossika offers sentence-based learning resources for several languages represented in this series. Individual course availability, free access, and paid features should be checked directly with the provider.

*Affiliate disclosure: WPMTest is a Glossika affiliate and may earn a commission when readers purchase through eligible referral links. No purchase is required to use WPMTest.*

**Editorial Commitment**

We aim to distinguish documented historical events from interpretation, recognize differences between languages and communities, and avoid portraying community-led revitalization as the achievement of an outside website.

We welcome corrections, appropriate linguistic review, and additional sources from people with relevant knowledge.
